subject: literature
passage: Miss Penhallow had let it be known, at every tea table in Ashcombe, that she thought the new schoolmaster's methods absurd: he took the children into the fields to count wildflowers, and he permitted them to ask questions in the middle of a lesson. When the parish council proposed that his salary be reduced, the vicar received an unsigned letter arguing, at considerable length and with some heat, that the village had never been better served. The vicar, who had exchanged notes with Miss Penhallow about the church flowers every week for twenty years, recognized the handwriting at once, and he folded the letter away without mentioning it to anyone. These details suggest that Miss Penhallow's public criticisms of the schoolmaster ______
stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: were shared by the vicar, who had long been her friend.
choices.B: did not fully reflect her view of his value to the village.
choices.C: had given way to approval of every one of his methods.
choices.D: expressed a sincere hope that he would soon leave Ashcombe.

explanation.why: The passage connects two details. The unsigned letter defends the schoolmaster warmly, and the vicar recognizes the handwriting from twenty years of Miss Penhallow's notes, so she wrote it. Her complaints at tea tables therefore did not tell the whole story of what she thought of him.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text never reveals the vicar's own view of the schoolmaster's methods.
explanation.B: Correct. Her unsigned letter, recognized by the vicar, praises the schoolmaster's service, so her public complaints were not the whole of her opinion.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The letter defends his value to the village; it does not show that she had come to approve of all his methods.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Her secret letter argues against cutting his salary, which hardly fits a wish for him to leave.
